The Farey Series

FractionsNumber TheorySequences
Game: A grid shows every fraction with a bottom number up to N as a dot you can see from the corner; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Press a dot under the diagonal, or use the arrow keys, to pick a fraction and see its two neighbours. Change N with the buttons.

Look for the math

The Farey series FN lists all fractions in lowest terms between 0 and 1 with denominators up to N, in order. For N = 5: 0/1, 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 2/5, 1/2, 3/5, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, 1/1.

Neighbours

If m₁/n₁ and m₂/n₂ are successive terms, then m₂n₁ − m₁n₂ = 1. The picture: the dot for p/q is at (q, p), and the fractions of FN are the dots you can see from the corner. That cross product is twice the area of the triangle formed by the corner and two neighbouring dots, so every such triangle has area exactly ½, the smallest a lattice triangle can have, and no other dot fits inside. The logic test checked this for every N from 2 to 70.

The middle one is a mediant

For three successive terms, m₂/n₂ = (m₁ + m₃)/(n₁ + n₃). The page proves it by subtracting the two neighbour equations (3): (m₃ + m₁)n₂ = m₂(n₃ + n₁). The page also goes back: start from 0/1 and 1/1, and keep inserting the mediant of two neighbours while its denominator is at most N, and you get exactly FN. The test did that for every N up to 70 and compared with a list made by sorting all fractions.

How many fractions

There are 1 + φ(1) + φ(2) + … + φ(N) terms, where φ counts the numbers up to n with no common factor with n; the test checked it for every N up to 70.

The applet's board draws every dot (q, p) with p and q up to N, so fractions above 1 appear above the diagonal. With One half off, each dot is also drawn with its two coordinates swapped. The page this puzzle is linked to is about the series itself, not the applet.

Pick 1/2 with N = 7 and see its neighbours. Then raise N to 8 and 9. When do the neighbours of 1/2 change?
